text:
Earth: Inner Core

Earth's inner core is a solid sphere composed primarily of iron and nickel.
Despite incredible pressure, temperatures of 5,400 degC (9,800 degF) keep it nearly
at melting point. It rotates slightly faster than the rest of Earth, creating
complex dynamics in Earth's magnetic field. The inner core is
1,221.5 km in radius.

Source (radius): Dziewonski & Anderson (1981), PREM, Phys. Earth Planet. Inter. 25:297.

Earth: Outer Core

The outer core is a liquid layer of iron, nickel, and lighter elements.
Convection currents in this highly conductive fluid generate Earth's
magnetic field through a process called the geodynamo. It extends from
1,221.5 to 3,480 km from Earth's center and has temperatures ranging from
4,500 degC (8,100 degF) to 5,400 degC (9,800 degF).

Source (radius): Dziewonski & Anderson (1981), PREM, Phys. Earth Planet. Inter. 25:297.

Earth: Lower Mantle

The lower mantle is composed of solid silicate rocks rich in iron and magnesium.
Despite being solid, it flows very slowly through convection, driving plate tectonics.
This region extends from 660 to 2,891 km below Earth's surface and experiences
temperatures from 2,200 degC to 4,500 degC (4,000 degF to 8,100 degF) and extreme pressure.

Source (boundaries): Dziewonski & Anderson (1981), PREM, Phys. Earth Planet. Inter. 25:297; Ishii et al. (2019), Nature Geoscience 12:869.

Earth: Upper Mantle

The upper mantle includes the asthenosphere, a partially molten layer where
most magma originates. This region flows more readily than the lower mantle,
allowing tectonic plates to move. It reaches from the base of the crust,
24.4 km below the surface in the reference model, down to
660 km, with temperatures from 500 degC to 2,200 degC
(900 degF to 4,000 degF).

Source (boundaries): Ishii et al. (2019), Nature Geoscience 12:869; Dziewonski & Anderson (1981), PREM, Phys. Earth Planet. Inter. 25:297.

Earth: Crust

Earth Crust
(Note: toggle off the crust layer in the legend to better see the interior structure.)

Earth's crust is the thin, solid outer layer where humans live. It's divided into
oceanic crust (5-10 km thick) made mostly of basalt, and continental crust (30-50 km thick)
made primarily of granite. The crust contains all known life and the accessible portion
of Earth's geological resources. Surface temperatures range from -80 degC to 60 degC (-112 degF to 140 degF).

Source (radius): IERS Conventions (2010), TN36 Table 1.1, equatorial radius; crust thicknesses: USGS, Interior of the Earth.

Earth: Lower Atmosphere

The lower atmosphere is drawn to the stratopause, 50 km up
(NOAA JetStream; NASA). It holds the troposphere (0-12 km) where weather occurs, and
the stratosphere (12-50 km) which contains the ozone layer. These regions contain
99% of atmospheric mass, primarily nitrogen and oxygen. Temperature varies from
about 15 degC (59 degF) at sea level to -60 degC (-76 degF) at the tropopause (12 km).
The stratopause (50 km) warms to near 0 degC (32 degF) due to ozone absorption.

Earth: Upper Atmosphere

The upper atmosphere is drawn from the stratopause (50 km) to the
thermopause, about 600 km up (NOAA JetStream; NASA). It includes
the mesosphere where meteors burn up and the thermosphere where the aurora occurs and
the International Space Station orbits. In the thermosphere, temperatures can reach
2,000 degC (3,600 degF), though the gas is so thin that it would feel cold to human skin.
Above the thermopause the exosphere thins into space with no boundary; its hydrogen
halo, the geocorona, is detected past 100 Earth radii.

Earth: Low Earth Orbit (LEO)

Low Earth Orbit (LEO)
Altitude range: 200 km to 2,000 km above surface
Radius: 6,578 km to 8,378 km from Earth's center (1.03 to 1.31 Earth radii)

LEO satellites orbit at all inclinations -- forming a true shell, not a ring.
One orbit takes 90-120 minutes; a satellite crosses the sky in ~6 minutes.

The bright moving points visible at dusk and dawn are LEO objects.
Starlink (~550 km), ISS (~400 km), and Hubble (~540 km) all live here.

Active satellites: ~11,000 (Starlink alone: ~7,000)
Tracked debris objects (>10 cm): 35,000+

Compare with the Geostationary Belt (GEO) at 42,164 km -- 5x farther out,
invisible to the naked eye, but controlling global communications.

Source (upper edge): IADC Space Debris Mitigation Guidelines, IADC-02-01 Rev. 3 (2021), sec. 3.3.2. The 200 km floor is a drawing choice, not a measured boundary.

Earth: Magnetosphere

Earth's magnetosphere extends about 10 Earth radii on the Sun-facing side
and stretches into a long magnetotail on the night side. It protects Earth
from solar radiation and cosmic rays, making complex life possible.

Source (standoff): Shue et al. (1998), J. Geophys. Res. 103:17691; Lugaz et al. (2016), Nat. Commun. 7:13001.

Earth: Bow Shock

Bow Shock: The boundary where the supersonic solar wind is first slowed
by Earth's magnetic field, typically located about 12.5 Earth radii upstream
from Earth on the Sun-facing side.
Drawn at the midpoint of the 11-14 R_E measured under normal solar wind (Lugaz et al. 2016).
The Bow Shock points towards the Sun along the X-axis. The XY plane is the ecliptic.

Source (standoff): Lugaz et al. (2016), Nat. Commun. 7:13001, doi:10.1038/ncomms13001.

Earth: Inner Radiation Belt

Inner Van Allen Belt: Region of trapped charged particles (mainly protons).
Drawn at the flux peak, 1.5 Earth radii from Earth's centre; the belt
spans roughly 1.1 to 2 Earth radii.
Source (peak): Baker et al. (2018), Space Sci. Rev. 214:17, doi:10.1007/s11214-017-0452-7.

Earth: Outer Radiation Belt

Outer Van Allen Belt: Region of trapped charged particles (mainly electrons).
Drawn at the flux peak, 4.5 Earth radii from Earth's centre; the belt
spans roughly 3 to 7 Earth radii and moves with geomagnetic activity.
Source (peak): J. Geophys. Res. Space Physics (2025), doi:10.1029/2024JA033504; Baker et al. (2018).

Earth: Geostationary Belt (GEO)

Geostationary Belt (GEO)
Altitude: 35,786 km / 0.000239 AU above surface
Radius: 42,164 km / 0.000282 AU from Earth's center (6.61 Earth radii)

Each point represents a region of this belt populated by active satellites.
Approximately 550 active geostationary satellites carry TV broadcasts,
weather imagery, communications, and GPS augmentation for half the world.

Apophis 2029: On April 13, 2029, Apophis passes at 38,013 km --
roughly 4,150 km INSIDE this belt. It will transit the sky as seen
from geostationary platforms and be visible to the naked eye from Earth.

Source: ITU, UCS Satellite Database, JPL CAD API

Earth: Hill Sphere

Earth's Hill Sphere (extends to about 235 Earth radii or about 1.5 million km)

The Hill sphere is the region around a body where its own gravity is the dominant force in attracting satellites. For
a planet orbiting a star, it's the region where the planet's gravity is stronger than the star's tidal forces.

The Hill Sphere radius can be described in words as follows: it is equal to the planet's average distance from the
Sun (its orbital semi-major axis) multiplied by the cube root of the ratio between the planet's mass and three times
the Sun's mass. In other words, you take how far the planet orbits out from the Sun, then scale that distance by the
cube root of (planet mass / [3 x solar mass]) to find the boundary within which the planet's gravity dominates over the Sun's.

Source (radius): derived from GM_Earth (IERS Conventions 2010) and GM_Sun (IAU 2015 B3) at a = 1 AU.

data.name: Earth-Moon Barycenter
text:
Earth-Moon Barycenter
Center of mass of the Earth-Moon system

Distance from Earth center: ~4,670 km
Distance below Earth surface: ~1,700 km
Location: between outer core and lower mantle

Why this matters:
Earth WOBBLES around this point every month!
The barycenter is inside Earth (unlike Pluto-Charon
where it's outside both bodies), but the wobble
is real and measurable.

The Sun-EMB Lagrange points (L1-L5) orbit
this point, not Earth's center. JWST, SOHO,
and other spacecraft 'orbit' a point defined
by this barycenter's path around the Sun.

Mass ratio: Moon/Earth = 1.23%
Highest of any planet-moon system!
(Compare: Io/Jupiter = 0.005%)

_encyclopedia.Moon:
Horizons: 301. Earth's only natural satellite. The Moon's orbit is actually inclined by about 5.145 deg to the ecliptic plane,
but approximately 28.545 deg to Earth's equatorial plane (this variation comes from Earth's own axial tilt of 23.4 deg).
The Moon's orbital parameters are not fixed but vary significantly over time due to precession of the nodes,
perturbations from the Sun's gravity, Earth's non-spherical shape, and other gravitational influences.

Missions: Early Pioneers (1950s-1960s):
* Luna Programme (USSR): This Soviet program launched many "Luna" probes, achieving significant firsts (1959 - 1966).
* Pioneer Program (USA): Early American attempts at lunar exploration. Pioneer 4 (1959) successfully performed a lunar flyby.
* Ranger Program (USA): A series of American impactor missions designed to take close-up images of the Moon before crashing into its surface (1961 - 1965).
* Surveyor Program (USA): American robotic landers that demonstrated the technology for soft landings, crucial for the Apollo program (1966 - 1968).
* Lunar Orbiter Program (USA): American orbiters that mapped the lunar surface in preparation for Apollo landings (1966 - 1967).
* The Apollo Era (1960s-1970s): NASA's iconic human spaceflight program that successfully landed humans on the Moon.n  * Apollo 8 (1968): First crewed mission to orbit the Moon.
  * Apollo 11 (1969): Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin became the first humans to walk on the Moon.
  * Five subsequent Apollo missions (Apollo 12, 14, 15, 16, 17) also landed astronauts on the Moon; Apollo 17, departing in December 1972.
* Renewed Robotic Exploration (1990s-Present): International Efforts.
  * Hiten (Japan, 1990): Japan's first lunar mission.
  * Clementine (USA, 1994): Orbiter that produced a detailed map of the lunar surface.
  * Lunar Prospector (USA, 1998): Orbiter that found evidence of water ice at the lunar poles.
  * SMART-1 (ESA, 2003): European Space Agency's first lunar mission, testing new propulsion technology.
  * Kaguya (SELENE) (Japan, 2007): Comprehensive lunar orbiter for scientific studies.
  * Chang'e Program (China): China's ambitious lunar exploration program (2007 - 2024).
  * Chandrayaan Program (India): India's lunar program (2008 - 2023).
  * Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter (LRO) (USA, 2009): NASA orbiter continuously mapping the Moon in high detail.
  * LCROSS (USA, 2009): Impact mission to search for water ice at the lunar poles.
  * GRAIL (USA, 2011): Twin spacecraft that precisely measured the Moon's gravity field.
  * LADEE (USA, 2013): Studied the lunar exosphere and dust.
  * CAPSTONE (USA, 2022): Tested a unique elliptical lunar orbit for future missions like the Gateway.
  * Commercial Lunar Payload Services (CLPS) (USA): NASA program funding private companies for lunar deliveries.
  * Luna 25 (Russia, 2023): Russia's first lunar landing attempt since 1976.
  * SLIM (Japan, 2024): Japan's successful, though sideways, lunar lander.
  * Queqiao-2 (China, 2024): A lunar communications relay satellite for far side missions.
* Future Missions (Ongoing and Planned):
  * Artemis Program (USA): NASA's program to return humans to the Moon, aiming for a sustained human presence.
  * Luna 26, 27, 28 (Russia): Planned future Russian lunar missions.
  * Beresheet2 (Israel): Planned private lunar mission.
  * Lunar Gateway: A planned international space station in lunar orbit, supporting future human missions.
_encyclopedia.Earth-Moon Barycenter:
Center of mass for the Earth-Moon system -- the highest mass ratio of any PLANET-moon system!

BINARY SYSTEM:
* Mass ratio: Moon/Earth = 1.23% (vs Charon/Pluto = 12.2%, Vanth/Orcus = 16%)
* The barycenter is INSIDE Earth (~4,670 km from center)
* That is ~1,700 km below the surface (73% from center to surface)
* Earth orbits barycenter at ~4,670 km radius (~0.0000312 AU)
* Moon orbits barycenter at ~379,730 km radius (~0.00254 AU)
* Period: 27.32 days

WHY THIS MATTERS:
* Earth WOBBLES around the barycenter every month
* This wobble affects Earth's heliocentric orbit (not a perfect ellipse!)
* The Sun-EMB Lagrange points (L1-L5) orbit THIS point, not Earth's center
* Compare: Pluto-Charon barycenter is OUTSIDE Pluto (true binary)

VISUALIZE:
* Select this as center, then select Earth and Moon
* Add Earth shells to see barycenter position in context
* The barycenter sits between outer core and lower mantle!

Horizons: 399. Our home planet, the third from the Sun.
* Earth-centered: do not select Earth; visualize shells at 0.02 AU.
* Heliocentric: select Earth with or without shells.
